1.1: 1.1 Argument. First it is to be seen why the apostle Paul in writing this epistle did not keep his custom of describing either the title of his name or the dignity of his rank. This is the reason: that writing to those who had believed from the circumcision, as apostle of the Gentiles and not of the Hebrews, knowing also their pride and showing his own humility, he did not wish to put forward the merit of his office. In a similar way John the apostle, on account of humility, in his epistle did not put forward his name for the same reason. This epistle written to the Hebrews the Apostle is said to have sent in the Hebrew language: the sense and order of which Luke the evangelist retained and, after the departure of blessed Paul the apostle, composed in Greek speech. Of old. It is not new. God, who is invariable then and now. Speaking. He says speaking, in the present, because what was then is also now. To the fathers. That is, to those who are fathers to us by flesh and by worship of God. By the prophets. For not they themselves, but God in them. At sundry times. That is many times to Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and the others, and often to the same. And in divers manners. Because now by dreams, as to Daniel: now by open voice, as to Moses: now by inward inspiration, as to David.
1.2: 1.2 By his Son, who is greater than the prophets. For the Lord is the fulfiller and sanctifier of the prophets. So he is a prophet, in that he is also the Lord of the prophets. So also Christ is an angel, as also the Lord of angels. Appointed immutably. Heir of all things, that is possessor of every creature. For no longer is Jacob the portion of the Lord, and Israel the lot of his inheritance: but absolutely all the nations of the world.
1.3: 1.3 Who being the brightness of his glory, etc. Here he commends Christ according to the divine nature, showing him coeternal and coequal with the Father, and of the same substance with him, but another in person. The figure of his substance. Behold, in another way personally, as the figure from him whose figure it is. But equal, because not unlike, as he himself says: The Father is in me; and: He that sees me sees my Father also, John 14. Note that these names, namely light, glory, are sometimes referred to the divine nature, sometimes to the person. And when they are referred to the person, now to the Father, now to the Son. For we say: The Father is light, and the Son is light. Likewise the Father is glory, the Son glory, and these two are one glory and one light, not two. And the Son is said to be glory of glory, as light of light, and principle of principle, and God of God, yet not two gods but one, not two principles but one. Brightness and figure, as also image, are properly referred to the person of the Son and are said relatively. And upholding all things, etc. It was said above that through him he made all things. Here he now attributes to him the highest authority, because with authority he governs and holds together all things. As all things were created by him, so by him unchangeable they are preserved. For the omnipotence of the Creator is the cause of subsisting for every creature, which power if it ever ceased from ruling the things it has made, at once the species and nature of all things would fall. Purgation. After he has shown his excellence by which he created and governs all things, here he commends the benignity of his humility. For he reminds us of the cross and resurrection and ascension, where he says: He sits, etc. On high. Saying this, he does not shut God up in place: but shows the man Christ higher than all and more eminent than all. So also by the right hand he did not deform God, but showed likeness of honor. For sitting shows nothing else but equality of honor.
1.4: 1.4 Being made so much better. Yet in the psalm he says: You have made him a little lower than the angels, Psalm 8. Here he is said to be better than the same. And as that was said according to the human nature, so this could be understood as said according to the divine, were not the effect added, whereby it is shown that here he speaks of him according to the flesh. For according to this, that he is acknowledged consubstantial with the Father's substance, he is not made but begotten: the discourse therefore is about him according to the human nature, according to which he was both less than the angels by the passion, and greater and better also by the fullness of grace, from which even the angels themselves receive by measure. A more excellent name. While he was mortal he had a different name, because the angels ministered to him. After he was immortal, more different. And because he could have this, and not above them, he adds before them, that is, greatly different from the name of angels, this is the name which is above every name, namely God, or Son, which in truth is more worthy than that by which they are called angels, that is messengers. For the name of Son shows property, not adoption, because unless he were the proper Son the Apostle could not from this assert the greatness of honor. The proper Son is begotten of the Father himself. If, however, he were Son by the grace of adoption, he would be less not only than the Father but also than the angels.
1.5: 1.5 This day. Lest the generation seem past, he said this day. For although that day also can be understood on which Christ was born according to the man, yet because today signifies presence, and in eternity nothing is past as if it had ceased to be, nor future as if it were not yet, but only present: because whatever is eternal always is: it is more divinely taken of the everlasting generation of the Wisdom of God, which the most sincere and Catholic faith proclaims. I will be to him. That is, his honor, or to that man to be born of the virgin. It can, however, be taken as said according to the flesh, for the flesh communicates with the higher things, as the divinity does with the lowly.
1.6: 1.6 Again he brings in, visible by the flesh assumed, who before was invisible in the world, which assumption is called a going forth from the Father: the bringing in to the inheritance, where he is commanded to be adored. And let them adore. And again the Father says of the same Son: When he brings in. That is, when he shows within, leading to the hearts of men by faith; what does he say? And let them adore. The angels adore, because they obey and reverence his command.
1.7: 1.7 Angels. Spirit is the name of nature; angel, of office. For those whom God made spirits, by sending as messengers he makes angels. And he uses all for the unchangeable decision of his purpose, whether the good by his grace or the evil by their own will. And by this the will of God is the first and highest cause of all bodily forms and motions. For nothing is done visibly which is not either commanded or permitted from the inward, invisible and intelligible court of the supreme Emperor, according to ineffable justice. Or those spirits are called angels when they are sent to announce light things: but when to vengeance, as in Sodom, they are called a burning fire. So also the ministers of the Church are fire while our vices are burned, but angels while they announce the word of God.
1.8: 1.8 But to the Son. Here by dignity and power together he commends Christ. For ever. Because he will always reign, and the last judgment will always stand; hence: These shall go into everlasting fire, and the others into life everlasting, Matthew 25.
1.9: 1.9 Has anointed you. According to the man, because the Deity needed nothing. The anointed signifies king or priest. God is repeated out of great love. Or according to Augustine: One case is the vocative, the other the nominative, thus: O you God the Son, your God has anointed you, namely the Father. In Latin the case is thought the same, but in Greek the distinction is most evident: by which the nominative is understood one way, the vocative another.
1.10: 1.10 And you. After the excellence of the humanity, he returns again to the eternity of the Son. In the beginning. Because the Creator exists before created things without any beginning. Of the hands. The power of command, that is the power of will, is called hand, because as he willed all things were made.
1.11: 1.11 They shall perish. From that which they are, while the creatures shall be changed for the better. But you shall remain. That as he is eternal before all things, so because he remains, he shall be the same after all things are changed. They shall grow old. To grow old is said of what is consumed like a garment, as human flesh, which yet shall be changed for the better.
1.12: 1.12 And as a vesture. It signifies the change of the heaven. Hence: I saw a new heaven and a new earth, Apocalypse 21. You shall change them, etc. Because the works of God shall stand under eternity, that they return not to corruption. But you, wholly unchangeable.
1.13: 1.13 To which of the angels. He undertakes to treat of the glory of the humanity. Sit. To the victorious Son the confession is offered by the Father. Of the feet. By the feet eternal stability is signified, that is, into eternity, where, the footprints being as it were set, he stands by the power of omnipotence.
1.14: 1.14 Are they not all, etc. As if to say: Surely. Understand therefore how great an honor is ours, that God destines his angels to us as ministers to friends. For although there is much difference between angels and men, yet he has made them near to us, because they care for our salvation, run to and fro for our sake, perform their office for us; this is the angelic work, the office of angelic function, that all things be done for the salvation of neighbors. This, however, is more the work of Christ, because he commanded the angels, our superiors, to render their ministry for our salvation.
2.1: 2.1 Therefore. After speaking of the Son of God many things that serve to commend him, he exhorts those to whom he writes to give diligent heed and keep the things announced to them through him. And to this all the foregoing tends, in which he proved that Christ was greater than the prophets and angels. More abundantly, than what was said of the law, or the prophets, or the angels. The Apostle is silent on the name of the law, because in his argument which he makes later he makes this also manifest. Let us slip away. We flow through the pains of mortal nature, we flow out by adding sins, we flow away entirely in eternal damnation. Hence he urges that the words of Christ be heard, by the punishment that will be for the negligent.
2.2: 2.2 And every transgression. He says every, that there be punishment for each sin; for not only will every transgressor who is guilty of many pay the penalty. A just recompense. He speaks so lest justice be thought to perish through mercy. What he says, retribution, refers to the quantity of the punishment, which will be equal to the sin: because according as the sin is greater or less, the punishment will be greater or less. What he says, of reward, refers to the quality of the punishment, so that he who perished by the fire of lust will be tormented by the fire of eternal burning.
2.4: 2.4 And by distributions of the Holy Spirit. By this he designates the abundance of graces, which was not among the ancients, neither such signs nor such diverse wonders, by which he shows that they were not simply believed, but through signs and wonders. And therefore when we believe, it is declared that we believe not them, but God.
2.6: 2.6 What is man. This can be read admiringly, so that by man and the Son of man Christ the man is understood. Of whom God was mindful in the conception, giving immunity from sin. And visited in the resurrection, giving the glory of immortality. It can also be read with disdain, of the earthly: for Adam was man, but not a son of man, as those are called men who bear his image. Those who bore the image of Christ are rather called sons of men. And that one is called the old man; this one, the new. Man in this place therefore is the earthly; but the Son of man, the heavenly. And that one is far removed from God, this one present. And therefore he is mindful of the former as of one placed far off. This one he visits whom he illumines with his countenance, that is by the presence of his grace. You visit him: man through the Son of man, as through a physician the sick, the Father visited.
2.7: 2.7 Glory. With the brightness of immortality, with honor, in that every knee is thus bent. Over the works of your hands, the more worthy, namely angels and men, which by excellence are called works of hands.
2.8: 2.8 In that he. He expounds David's sense. David says, Psalm 8: You have subjected all things: In that Scripture subjected, that is, showed all things subjected, he left nothing, that is, excepted nothing of all.
2.9: 2.9 But him, etc. The angels can be called greater than man, because they are greater than the body of man. They are greater also in mind, but only in this, that by the merit of original sin the body weighs down the soul itself; but this is not so in Christ. As for what seems to you, that nothing great is said of God the Father if the form of a servant is greater, by which even the angels seem greater; you do not think rightly, nor do you attend what place human nature has among things, which was made to the image of God: to which, however, no injury was done when Christ said: The Father is greater than I, John 14.; who preferred God the Father not only to his flesh but also to the human mind which he bore, which without doubt is recognized as the form of a servant, since the whole creation serves the Creator. On account of the passion. Here he begins to show that the words of Christ are to be heard not only for power or vengeance, but for the love with which he loved us, that he might die for us.
2.10: 2.10 The author. Christ. Of their salvation, that is, of the sons. For he is Son by nature, of whom we shall be heirs who are sons by adoption. See how great he is in the midst of us: He is Son, and we are sons. But there is a difference, that he saves, we are saved. He sanctifies, we are sanctified. Now Scripture joins us, now separates. Many sons, it says, here he joined: the author of their salvation, here he distinguished. Through suffering. Because unless Christ died, man would not be redeemed, and not redeemed would perish. Which, if it were so, all things would have been made in vain. For the rest serve man, man serves God. Nor would God be glorified in any, since all things were made for this. The predestination also concerning bringing many sons would be false. To consummate. This began in the resurrection, when he was exalted by the glory of immortality. And increased in the ascension, when he ascended to the right hand of the Father. And will be perfected at the judgment, when all things shall be subjected to him, and he shall be all in all, 1 Corinthians 15. For he who, etc. AUGUSTINE. He proves that it befitted Christ to suffer for our deliverance, etc., down to since it is agreed that he knew each nature of himself. All of one. But he as proper Son, we adoptive. When he says: he is not ashamed to call them brethren, he shows that our fraternity with him is not of nature but of mercy. Which he proves by the prophet, lest it be thought new.
2.14: 2.14 Because therefore. As if: Since all were of one, and because the children who were to be sanctified had partaken of flesh, that is were men of soul and body, which is understood by blood, corruptible; therefore he himself also, Christ, partook of the same children, or of the same, that is flesh and blood, and this likewise, that is passible and mortal, that he might die, and so destroy the devil, and by death make the law void, and make the Jews free by grace who by fear of punishments were slaves of the law. Through death. A wonder indeed! Death was the arms by which the devil conquered, and by it the devil was conquered by Christ.
2.16: 2.16 Nowhere. He partook of the same to sanctify men. And rightly this cause is added, because if he were not going to free them, he would not partake with them. Which appears in the angels, because nowhere, that is, no Scripture is read to have taken hold of angels. He took hold. The Apostle said: took hold, not assumed, as if: He overtook one fleeing far. In which can be understood the dignity of human nature, and the mercy and grace by which he did it, and the care he had of us. For human nature was fleeing before, and fleeing far (for we were far); pursuing he took hold, this dignity was given not to angelic but to human nature, that God should be joined to it in one person.
2.17: 2.17 In all things. Because he was born, brought up, grew; suffered, died. Who is above called the figure of the Father's substance.
2.18: 2.18 For in that. That is, in the flesh which he took he suffered many cruel things. And he knows by experience what this tribulation of the suffering is. Who are tempted. God tempts to prove, the devil to deceive, man to know what he does not know.
3.1: 3.1 Wherefore, brethren. He infers from all the above; as if: Because he is powerful, because he suffered for us, and can help.
3.2: 3.2 Who is faithful. He begins to compare Christ with Moses, as above with the prophets and angels, so that he is faithful before Moses, because he sought not his own but the Father's glory, nor hid his commands. Which Christ is faithful to the Father (as Moses) in all the house of the Jews and Gentiles.
3.3: 3.3 Of greater. As if: That he was faithful the very effect shows: because he is worthy of glory, like Moses: and indeed of greater than Moses, that is, than Moses, or beyond Moses in merit.
3.4: 3.4 For every house, etc. I say fabricated, for it cannot be made by itself, but by someone. Is it therefore by Christ? Truly, because it is God who makes the house, and all things. But he who created all things, and the house, is God. For of each house, both that which Moses ruled and that which Christ built, God is the maker.
3.5: 3.5 And Moses. He shows Christ worthy of greater glory than Moses, because Christ is the builder of the house, not Moses. Here he shows another reason also, namely that Christ is the son, Moses a servant, who delivered carnal things to the carnal, but Christ spiritual things.
3.7: 3.7 Wherefore. Since above he had commended Christ before the angels and prophets in many things, he added that we ought to observe the things we have heard from him; so now, Christ being commended before Moses, he begins to terrify them, lest they be unbelieving to Christ by the likeness of the fathers; and lest they lose the rest, he flatters them by the opportunity of the time. Today. Now he speaks by himself, who before spoke by heralds: if then you were hard, be soft now.
3.8: 3.8 Harden not your hearts; that is, be not rebellious and stubborn to God, but obedient.
3.9: 3.9 They tempted; that is, they sought out of curiosity.
3.10: 3.10 Offended. Greatly and implacably angry. Hostile. Or near to applying the scourges of correction.
3.11: 3.11 In my wrath. God is said to be angry by the figure anthropopathy. If they shall enter into my rest. It is aposiopesis, that is, they shall not enter.
3.12: 3.12 An evil heart of unbelief. That you may think Christ is not sufficient without the law, which is evil, because so man falls into many sins. Nor is this light, because this is the heart of departing from the living God.
3.13: 3.13 Until today; that is, the time of grace, and of which the prophet spoke above in the psalms, because grace is not offered less now to believers for salvation than when Christ was present bodily. The deceitfulness of sin, that is of the devil, who is the cause of sin.
3.14: 3.14 For we are made partakers of Christ. You ought to exhort and not be hard, because what we were not, we have been made by grace, having a part with Christ in the inheritance: yet on this condition, if the beginning of the substance, that is of faith, which is the beginning of goods, through which God exists in us, and through which we are deified, and partake of the divine substance, we hold firm to the end.
3.16: 3.16 For some, hearing. He says this lest anyone think it enough to hear about the rest, because they all heard, but not all heard, and not all arrived.
4.2: 4.2 Profited not, etc. For having come out of Egypt, when they had traveled a long way and received many proofs of the power of God in Egypt, in the Red Sea, in the wilderness, they made a plan to send spies who should look over the nature of the land. What they heard. By the spies; who brought back evil things, they did not believe; or distinguish thus, of faith received from the things they heard.
4.3: 4.3 And indeed. He here treats what the first rest signifies. Works. Because he had said that rest was announced, he says when: namely, before the law, after the completion of the works of seven days through the rest of the sabbath; and under the law, when it was designated through the promised land; and in the time of grace, the Holy Spirit saying in David: today, etc., as if, rest was announced and so indeed when the fulfillment of that true rest was not yet signified, because no one had yet obtained rest. Finished. Which was when man was made, for whom all things were made, and he himself was made to glorify God.
4.4: 4.4 And he rested on the seventh day. In six days he made all things, so that afterward nothing would be made except from the matter then made, and in likeness of what was made. On the seventh day he rested, which therefore signifies rest. So also in the sixth age Christ the man was born into the world to labor, on the sixth day and in the sixth hour of the day he suffered, on the seventh he rested. So also we, while we live under the works of six days, work; going out thence, we rest: if only our works be found very good.
4.5: 4.5 And in this place. Of the second rest, which is signified by the figure of the rest of the promised land.
4.7: 4.7 Again he limits a certain day, today. Of the third signified, and when it is given, though obscurely, which was promised through Christ to believers. After so long a time. In this it is plain that this is another rest of which David says today, than that to which Joshua led. For if that were it, David would not speak of another; therefore it is certain that there is another to which Christ leads, which Palestine signified through that.
4.8: 4.8 To them, the children of Israel, to whom rest was first announced by a sign, that is the promised land; he would never have given rest, that is at no time; afterward, that is in the following time; he would speak of another day, that is the time of grace, in which it was to be given. Or, he would never afterward speak of another, namely rest, besides the promised land. In saying, this day he means the same as he had said above, today, etc.
4.9: 4.9 A sabbatism; that is, the true rest signified by the sabbath (that is, the festal joy of full quiet) in which the Lord rested and which was observed in the law. For then we shall perfectly be at leisure, refreshed with greater grace and filled with God. And we shall know perfectly that he is God. There we shall be at leisure, we shall see, and we shall love. We shall love and praise: behold what shall be in the end without end. For what other end is ours than to come to the kingdom which has no end?
4.11: 4.11 Into the same example. Or, into such a punishment as they had through unbelief; he says example that we may keep our mind there, lest we fall likewise.
4.12: 4.12 The word of God. Which comes from the royal seats. Living. Whom the unbelieving think dead. Piercing. Reaching with its whole consideration to the separation of the soul, that is sensuality, and the spirit, that is reason. Division of soul. By soul we live with the beasts, by spirit we understand with the angels. And therefore by soul are understood carnal sins, that is those done by act of the body, like luxury. By spirit spiritual ones, that is those of the mind, like pride. The word of God discerns between carnal and spiritual sins: who does what, with what mind. And spirit. The word of God pierces with inseparable knowledge, because it knows how sensuality is divided from reason, and each from itself, while, given more to lowest things, it is lower, or, recalled from them, more worthy. So also it sees how the spirit is divided from itself, whether while it gapes at God thinking of the divine vision, or while it considers heavenly things lower, or lower on earth treats of rightly doing worldly things, or how the spirit, that is reason, is separated from sensuality, while what is lower in itself overcomes what is higher in that. Also joints. A joint is the juncture itself of sensuality and reason, which the Son of God sees; namely how they cohere with each other in something, either this and that, that is reason and sensuality, how in their differences they agree with each other, while the higher difference of sensuality, consenting, agrees with the differences of reason. Or the lower difference of reason, pressed and captive, sometimes consents to the lower difference of sensuality. Of marrow. The marrow which is inmost is here called whatever is more inward and subtle in the soul or spirit, which the Son of God also sees. For he discerns thoughts, that is what different men think of different things. He discerns also the intentions of those thoughts, whither each tends, to good or evil. And, to say more, no creature, earthly or heavenly, is invisible to him, but all things are naked and open, because on every side fully seen. Likewise joints he calls the conjunctions of thoughts: marrow the intentions of them.
4.14: 4.14 Having therefore. Here he begins to speak of the high priest Christ, how sufficient, and how more worthy than the old priest. Whom he also changes, and the law that is under him, by his better law, and how necessary to us for justice and salvation.
4.15: 4.15 For we have not, etc. As if: Let us hold, and we ought to hold, because, being powerful, he is also merciful, having experienced our infirmity. Who cannot, etc. It is impossible for a man who has not had experience of affliction and has not sensibly endured all things to know the afflictions of the afflicted. But Christ knows not only because he is God, according to which he knows all things, but because he is man and endured like things.
4.16: 4.16 In seasonable help. Now is the time of help, now is the time of gifts, when those sinning after baptism can find penance through grace. But when the bridal chamber shall be shut, when the king shall have entered to see the guests, so that those worthy of it have come to the bosom of the patriarch, then for the wicked will be the time of despair. But now, while the contest still remains and the palm hangs, one must not despair, but approach with confidence, that is without doubting, that through grace it may be approached, seasonable help found. For there is a time that is not fitting.
5.1: 5.1 For every high priest. Because spiritual things do not so introduce the weak as do bodily things, he begins with these, wishing to show that the New Testament is better than the Old. Some things he puts common to Christ with priests, some higher belonging to Christ alone. Others, again, lower, suited to those priests only.
5.2: 5.2 Because he himself also. Take away here the occasion of exalting oneself above others.
5.4: 5.4 Neither does any man, etc. He strikes the covetous, who are not called but thrust themselves in.
5.5: 5.5 Christ did not glorify himself. The Son was glorified by the Father when he said: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased, Matthew 3. Which glorification was foretold long before through the Prophet: You are my Son, this day have I begotten you, Psalm 2.
5.6: 5.6 You are a priest. Christ is a priest, not according to the fact that he is born of the Father God with God, coeternal with the begetter: but on account of the flesh assumed, on account of the victim which he offered for us. According to the order of Melchizedek, who was not temporal, Scripture being silent on the beginning and end of his life, in figure of Christ who lacks beginning and end. And as he offered in bread and wine and once, so Christ also under the species of bread and wine gave his body and blood to the disciples.
5.7: 5.7 Prayers and supplications. He speaks of the action and life of Christ, of which every action of the faithful is an instruction, and prayer to God. Whatever Christ did were prayers and supplications for all. The shedding of blood was the strong cry, in which he was heard, for the reverence of the same passion. The reverence is that he suffered without sin for charity alone. He was heard. By this it is plain that through him we can obtain mercy, since he is now at the right hand of the Father.
5.8: 5.8 He learned, etc. That is, he voluntarily took on obedience unto death.
5.9: 5.9 To all that obey. So great is the power of the passion that it suffices for all for salvation, which salvation can well be through him, because he is called, etc. He was made the cause of salvation, not of any whatever, but eternal; not for few but for all; on this condition, however, that they obey him. For otherwise they will not be able to obtain salvation. And he can well be the cause of salvation to the rest, since he is called by God a high priest, as he himself also really shows by his works that he is such. For because he fulfilled the office of high priest, and was obedient to the Father in all things, and in himself arrived at so great a consummation of all goods that he sufficed also for the salvation of others, therefore he is called by God a high priest, and this according to the order of Melchizedek, namely that every order of divinity may be considered in him, which could be considered in Melchizedek.
5.11: 5.11 Hard to be interpreted. The discourse on the incarnate Son is difficult to interpret, because you are weak in sense for understanding deep mysteries.
5.12: 5.12 For whereas you ought. He inserts a rebuke of weakness, that they may labor to understand the high things of Christ. What are the elements of the beginning. The beginning of the discourses is simple doctrine. Its elements, the matter it treats, such as the birth, the passion.
5.13: 5.13 For every one, etc. He who does not grasp this: The Word was made flesh, how will he grasp: In the beginning was the Word? Every discourse on this matter in which it is treated that it be not only believed but also understood, and what is said be known, is burdensome: it presses them more easily than it feeds them. Hence it happens that the spiritual do not wholly keep silent about these things to the carnal, because of the Catholic faith, which must be preached to all. Yet they do not so abandon them as, wishing to lead them to an understanding they cannot hold, to make them sooner loathe the discourse in the truth than perceive the truth in the discourse.
6.1: 6.1 Wherefore. Having sharply rebuked and blamed them because they want always to learn the same things, he again flatters them by counting himself with them, exhorting them to perfection. The word of the beginning of Christ, by which the unlearned are to be catechized, such as the Creed and the Lord's Prayer. Not again, that is not formerly, that as before they fell, they may fall again. Or, not laying again, let us so lay now that there be no more need to lay. The foundation. What he first called the word of the beginning, he here calls the foundation, because it is set forth first to those coming to the Christian religion, that upon this what belongs to perfection may be built. This foundation is divided into six, which are: the beginning or penance, faith, the doctrine of baptisms, imposition of hands, resurrection, and judgment. Whoever converts anyone to the faith first makes him repent, believe in God, be baptized for remission, be confirmed by imposition, and look for the resurrection and the day of judgment.
6.4: 6.4 It is impossible. Lest anyone think that a second or third baptism can be had after sins, he adds: Impossible, not merely difficult, lest anyone should trust in this. Those who, that is, even those who have had these goods. Still less the utterly wicked.
6.6: 6.6 To be renewed, by baptism, whose power consists in the cross of Christ, whence it is added: Crucifying again. Because in baptism we are conformed to his death and burial. He who thinks to be baptized a second time crucifies Christ a second time (as far as he is concerned), which is to hold him up to shame and derision; as he died once, so we die once to sins in baptism, not a second or third time.
6.7: 6.7 Which often comes. He says often coming, because if rare it does not suffice: if constant, it grows cheap. The rain. Holy doctrine, the dew of heaven, which the heavens, that is the preachers of the word of truth, rain on the thirsty earth. Bringing forth herb. It signifies that they often drank through the law and the prophets the word of heavenly doctrine, who yet were not so ready to bring forth the shoots of faith. By whom it is tilled. The tillers of the earth are those who with the spiritual plowshare cut up the shrubs, and with the pruning-hook of the word of God cut off what is harmful. Or those by whom it is tilled are those same who cultivate themselves in good works, imitating, namely, their elders, according to that: And they made the fruit of their birth, because they imitate their fathers, who begot them in the faith.
6.9: 6.9 We are confident. Because for the present the Apostle has nothing for which to praise them; he lifts them up by hope of future things, to which he allures by past things, and revives their spirits and comforts them, recalling ancient things to their mind, and makes them think that God has not forgotten the goods they did. For as the former goods had been made dead and void by the evils that followed, so these same by penance and other goods that follow will revive.
6.10: 6.10 Of the work. He testified great things of them. Three goods he commends in them, namely that they made all their goods common to the saints. Behold the work, and this from love, which informs actions; behold the readiness, and this for the glory of God; behold the pure and right intention.
6.11: 6.11 We desire. He shows great love toward them, and shows the same care for each one, and takes care alike of greater and lesser, and loves all.
6.13: 6.13 For Abraham, etc. He says three things: that the promise was made; and was confirmed by oath; and in Abraham was already fulfilled.
6.14: 6.14 Unless blessing, etc. It is aposiopesis here, that is a breaking off. As if: If I do not do this, let me not be believed in anything.
6.17: 6.17 Wherein more abundantly willing. As if he said: If a man, who is a liar, is believed by oath, how much more should God be believed, who cannot lie?
6.18: 6.18 We flee for refuge. He flees to hope who, by the hope of beatitude, scorns tribulations.
6.19: 6.19 Which as. As an anchor holds a ship, so hope holds the soul, that it be not drowned in the sea of this world by consenting to iniquity; and firm, that it may not even waver. AUGUSTINE. Cast your care upon God, etc., down to if for a time it is tossed, hope is its anchor.
6.20: 6.20 Forerunner. For this Christ ran before, that we may follow. Who is well called a runner, because no fault hindered him, according to that: He rejoiced as a giant to run the way, Psalm 18. And elsewhere: In the way of sinners he stood not, ibid. 1. And forerunner, because he ran before us and for us.
7.1: 7.1 Priest of the most high God. CHRYSOSTOM, hom. 35 on Genesis. He was a priest perhaps ordained by himself, for so priests were then. Or because he was advanced in age, he was honored by his own. Or because he himself also was eager to sacrifice, as Noah, Abel, Abraham, when they offered sacrifices.
7.3: 7.3 Neither beginning, etc., nor end of life. Christ had altogether no beginning nor end. For ever. He says this because Scripture is silent that anyone succeeded him. Or he speaks mystically of the priesthood of Christ.
7.4: 7.4 Now consider, etc. He lingers in commending the dignity of Melchizedek and the excellence of his priesthood; preferring him to Abraham himself, the father of all, and to all the Levites.
7.5: 7.5 And indeed of the sons of Levi, etc. As if: And from this consider how great he is, because some of the sons of Levi by this that they receive the sacrifice (for otherwise they would not dare) have a commandment in the law, without whose authority they would never presume to take tithes.
7.8: 7.8 It is testified. As I, or, the same in many places. He lives. For he bore the type of our high priest, whose excellence of power is shown by his likeness. For through Melchizedek, in whom the figure went before, the priesthood of Christ is distinguished from the priesthood of Levi; in the figure of Christ it is said that Melchizedek lives. Hence he is called a priest forever, who offered himself, not from any necessity, but from the will of his own power.
7.11: 7.11 Under it. Because the law is in the hand of the priest, and through him the law is fulfilled which is said to consummate. This translation was prefigured in Samuel, who of the tribe of Ephraim was chosen priest by the Lord, the sons of Eli being rejected, the Lord saying: He that honors me, I will honor; and he that dishonors me, etc.
7.12: 7.12 For the priesthood being translated, etc. That another arises he subsequently proves both by the tribe and by the rite. By the tribe there: Of whom these things, etc. By the rite there: And yet more, etc. The priesthood being translated. Because therefore law and priesthood were given alike, and by the same, and under the same promise, what is said of the one must be understood of the other.
7.14: 7.14 For it is evident, etc. The priesthood was translated from tribe to tribe, from the priestly to the royal, that the same may be priestly and royal. And consider the mystery: first it was royal, afterwards it became priestly. So Christ was always king; he was made priest when he took flesh, when he offered sacrifice.
7.16: 7.16 Not according to the law. That is according to the carnal understanding of the law, to do according to carnal observances; but according to the power of the law itself, that is the spiritual understanding, which those who follow have eternal life. There is a difference between priesthood and priesthood. That carnal, this spiritual. That temporal, this eternal.
7.22: 7.22 By so much. From the praise of the priest he infers the commendation of the law. Better. Because it promises better, that is eternal things; the Old Testament, however, temporal.
7.24: 7.24 But this, etc. As Christ remains, so also the law which he brought, in which is true remission of sins and perpetual grace, which because the old law could not give, it was excluded. That it remains forever he shows from the priest, who is one, which he would not be unless he were immortal, as in the law there were many, because mortal.
7.25: 7.25 Whereby also he is able to save. It being shown that through the priesthood of Christ the old priesthood and law are destroyed, he commends his act by depressing, by contrast, the operation of the old priesthood.
7.26: 7.26 Holy, inwardly. Innocent, in hands. Undefiled, in body. Separated from sinners, that is free from all sin.
7.27: 7.27 Who needs not, etc. Being such, he has no necessity to offer daily. The Apostle did not say this as though Christ ever needed it, but to remove from him what befits others. For he did this once by offering himself. So great is the sacrifice that, though offered once, it suffices for eternity.
7.28: 7.28 For the law makes men, etc. They have necessity to offer daily, because weak; this one offering himself once suffices for all, because perfect.
8.1: 8.1 The chief point. CHRYSOSTOM. The apostle Paul mingles lowly things with exalted, always following his Master, etc., down to who ought to perform the office of priest. We have such. Here begins the chapter; and it ends there: God and not man. In the heavens. Or above the material heavens. Or, above thrones and dominations.
8.2: 8.2 A minister of the holies. Because he ministers to the saints increase of virtues and eternal life. Or, in heaven he ministers glory signified by the holy of holies. Minister of the true tabernacle. That is of the truth, which the old tabernacle prefigured; namely justice in the present Church, glory in the future. Which true tabernacle God pitched, that it may remain forever; the shadowy one was not pitched but portable; and not man: he adds this because the old one God also set up, but by a man as minister.
8.3: 8.3 What he may offer. And since it is necessary that he have something to offer; either it will be on earth or heavenly: but not on earth, because if so he would not be a priest; therefore what he offers is heavenly.
8.4: 8.4 If he were, etc. If then he were, etc. Because everyone who offers, if there were any earthly one who could cleanse the human race, he would not be a priest according to the order of Melchizedek, because there would be enough to offer legal things; but because those were mortal and sinners, and therefore not able to cleanse the human race, Christ came, who would suffice. But now, that is in the last age, Christ has obtained a better ministry of priesthood as much as his law is better. Now from the priesthood and sacrifice he passes to the difference of the Testaments.
8.5: 8.5 It was answered, etc. Not when he was beginning, because he had already expressed many things in figures, but when he could not by himself consummate, he consults the Lord, who taught him of the figures as well as of the truth.
8.6: 8.6 And of a better Testament, etc. Now from sacrifice and priesthood he passes to the difference of the Testaments, preferring the New to the Old; because the New is established on better promises.
8.7: 8.7 For if that former. He proves that the Testament of Christ is better than the Old: for that is not free of fault, this is free. For if it had been free of fault, a second would not be given, but it is given. And so it appears that that was imperfect, this perfect. Fault would have been absent, certainly not. He says this as though it had fault. Which is seen when it commands without grace and makes transgressors. Would be sought, by the Lord, who first gradually instructed and brought up, that afterward he might give the perfect.
8.9: 8.9 Which I made with their fathers. And because he had made a special one with some, he determines. Which I made in the day, that is the time of the law, which was given after the exit from Egypt. What he said before the law to Abraham: In your seed shall all nations be blessed, Genesis 22., he afterwards fulfilled in the Gospel. For that promise was spiritual and specially pertaining to grace. They continued not in my Testament. He ascribes to their fault that they did not continue in the Testament, lest the law which they then received seem blameworthy. For it is that which Christ came not to destroy but to fulfill. Yet it does not justify without grace, because of the harm of the old man, which because it is not healed by the letter commanding and threatening, that is called the Old; this the New: on account of the newness of the spirit which heals from the vice of oldness, which he evidently opens, saying: This is the Testament, etc.
8.10: 8.10 Giving my laws into their minds. Not on tables of stone, not with ink, but by the Spirit, by whose presence (who is the finger of God) charity is poured out in hearts, which is the fullness of the law. For the just are not terrified from outside, but love justice within. Giving laws: Behold the Testament. I will write above. As if: Which ought to rise above and rule them. And I will be to them a God. That is they shall live from me and for me, and in the future shall see me, which is perfection, so that one teach not another. This is the difference between the Old and the New, that that is on stone, this on the heart; there the reward, the land; here the vision of God.
8.11: 8.11 They shall not teach. What lay hidden in the letter, and the people learned by the traditions of masters, this the Spirit coming taught the apostles, and this is what the Prophet says: They shall teach no more every one his neighbor, because all shall know me, Jeremiah 31.; as in the Gospel it is said: Then he opened their understanding, Luke 24., etc. To the greatest. Understand the greater either in time: as the first who awaited us the later in receiving the denarius; or the more worthy in knowledge or virtue, who namely were able to understand the incorporeal and unchangeable light, as far as can be in this life: which the lesser, however, were able to believe. When therefore that which is perfect shall come, and that which is in part shall be done away, then he who, taking flesh, appeared in the flesh, will show himself to those who love him. Then all shall know him from the least to the greatest, because even the least will then know perfectly, when he shall be instructed by himself, not by a greater.
9.1: 9.1 It had. Thus far he has shown the difference of the Testaments, and that the New surpasses the Old and changes it. Now he shows the same from the plan of the tabernacle itself. A sanctuary, not spiritual but: Worldly. Because it was thought holy by men. And truly it had a worldly sanctuary, because the first and second tabernacle.
9.2: 9.2 For there was a tabernacle made, the holy. The first tabernacle had within the altar of incense; before the doors, in the open air, the altar of holocausts: or what is outside signifies the Old Testament, and is the figure of a figure; what is within signifies the New.
9.5: 9.5 Cherubim. By the Cherubim is signified fullness of knowledge; by the propitiatory over the ark, Christ, because to Christ himself it was specially given by God the Father to be the propitiation for our sins.
9.7: 9.7 Once a year. That it was entered every year signified that perfection had not yet come. For his own and the people's ignorance. Christ offered for his people, but for himself not, except in his members. Hence he himself says: The words of my offenses, Psalm 21. For he calls our offenses his, because he took them, not to keep them but to destroy them.
9.8: 9.8 Not yet made manifest. Heaven is still inaccessible to mortals according to the condition of the body, and before even according to souls. But the resurrection is to be awaited patiently, in which also to bodies the access to heaven will lie open through Christ. The way of the holies. The way of the holies is Christ, or the spiritual understanding of the law through which one ascends to the interior of heaven.
9.9: 9.9 Which is a parable. That these things about sacrifices to be completed, either in the first or in the second tabernacle, were said according to signification, he opens, adding: which is a parable, etc.
9.10: 9.10 Until the time of correction; that is until the time of grace, in which those who till then were under the pedagogue were to be corrected for the better, whom the law could not make perfect, yet it was not to cease at that time.
9.11: 9.11 By a greater. Christ entered the tabernacle, that is heaven. By the name of the sign, that is the tabernacle, the Apostle designates the thing signified, that is heaven, which is well said to be greater, because it holds more than that earthly one, and more perfect, because there is perfect beatitude.
9.12: 9.12 Into the holies. He expounds what he had said: A tabernacle not made by hand, the holy of holies, that is heavenly things.
9.13: 9.13 For if the blood. That redemption could be through Christ he proves from the lesser, because by those legal things bodily cleansing was effected. Of goats. The goat signifies Christ, by the likeness of sinful flesh. The bull is called Christ, because with the horns of the two Testaments he tosses his enemies. To the cleansing of the flesh, that is, that the flesh may be cleansed on account of the precept of the law; but in Christ is perfection.
9.14: 9.14 Offered himself. Christ, mediator between God and men, is the giver of the New Testament: as high priest he is the giver of the new law to us. Without spot. His blood is spotless. From dead works; that is sins, which whoever touches is defiled, as he who touched a dead body was defiled; nor does he enter heaven, as neither did he the temple. To the living. Yet the death of Christ was necessary in the redemption not only of the Gentiles, but also of those transgressions which the law showed and did not remove. So great was our sin that we could not be saved unless the Only-begotten of God died for us, debtors to death; but thus he made us worthy of the Testament and the promised inheritance, and thus the Testament was made firm.
9.15: 9.15 Death intervening. Between the Old Testament and the New (in which not only the sacraments are divided but also the promises) the distinction is the passion of Christ, in whose death it is established that earthly things are not promised, but eternal. For in the death of the Only-begotten great things must be hoped.
9.16: 9.16 For where. Christ is the giver of the New Testament, death intervening, and now for the confirmation of the Testament Christ could die, as he proves by the custom of human law.
9.19: 9.19 Wool. The charity of Christ is for us wool, from which we make a garment.
9.22: 9.22 And without shedding of blood, etc. This qualification is added because by the water of sprinkling made from the ashes of the red heifer remission of sins was sometimes made when blood was not shed, though yet it had been shed in the immolation of the heifer. In those sacrifices, however, although they were imposed on a perverse people more suitably than offered to a God who desired them, yet they were a figure of the truth, which is Christ, by whose blood we are redeemed and cleansed, because our cleansing and God's propitiation for us is none without blood.
9.23: 9.23 The heavenly things themselves. Christ, who was signified in some things, did not need to be cleansed, but all his own need it; yet his signs, which in the tabernacle served the use of ministration, were cleansed with blood.
9.25: 9.25 Nor yet that he should offer often, etc. He proved that Christ cleansed heavenly things by his victim; now he proves that by better victims, that is that his victim was more worthy and efficacious than all others: because those often repeated without consummation, this once offered leads back to the fatherland.
9.26: 9.26 Otherwise, etc. If once offered he did not suffice to drain the sins of all believing in him, he ought to have suffered more often from the beginning of the world; which, lest it be so, he suffered once in the consummation of the ages. In the consummation. That is, in the last age in which all things are fulfilled that before were imperfect, and therefore there was no need that he begin to suffer from the beginning of the world.
9.27: 9.27 And as. The natural law shows this, which has been proved by the inconvenient. Once to die. It is not to be understood that Christ was offered by any necessity of his own sin, even once, but by will alone. But as a man once dead by necessity and by the right of nature dies no more, so Christ by the same right once offered cannot die any more. But after this. After once dying, judgment remains, in which all receive according to what they have deserved; but it does not remain that they rise again and die anew.
9.28: 9.28 Shall appear without sin. So that then there will be no victim for sin, but justice in rewarding or condemning. For if on the day of wrath there will be no victim, much less at other times. Or without sin, that is the likeness of sinful flesh, but rather in glorious flesh.
10.1: 10.1 For the law having a shadow. He proved that Christ was once dead; but why? why once? Because the law could not make perfect, therefore a lamb without blemish was to be offered. Not the very image. That is the truth, as in painting, until one lays on the colors there is a certain underdrawing. Or the underdrawing is a certain shadow and not an image; but when one has dyed in the very colors of the flowers, then the image is made. Comers. Although the high priests offered every year into the holy of holies with the same victims unceasingly, they could never be made perfect by their victims.
10.2: 10.2 Worshipers once, etc. One victim of Christ makes perfect; and if thousands sin they need no other, because it suffices for all, and washes every conscience from sins; which the old did not, for if it had done this, there would be no need to repeat it. As a medicine, if it be strong and effective for health and able to drive off every ailment, applied once works the whole; but if it is always applied, it is manifest proof that it has not brought health; and therefore because by those sacrifices no one was cured, they were frequently offered.
10.3: 10.3 A commemoration, not an absolution; an accusation of weakness, not a showing of power; for the sake of showing weakness, therefore, and that a memory of sins might be made, God commanded those to be always offered.
10.5: 10.5 You would not. From the time of the passion, in which is the consummation of all victims, they began to displease. He never destroyed them before, but was subject to them while he was presented in the temple with victims. But a body you have fitted to me. The signs were taken away, because the truth was shown, then it was time that those be taken away and the truth come. Nor did the Lord ever delight in those odors, except in the faith and desire of the offerer. Yet he commanded these to be offered to him rather than that they be offered to idols; and imposed them for servitude, not for justification, and that they be a figure of the future.
10.6: 10.6 They pleased not. In those figures the truth was foretold. They celebrate figures, many knowing the thing of the figures, but more ignorant of what ought to cease when the thing is shown.
10.7: 10.7 Then. When I saw all those displease, and a body fit for this given me. I said: Behold I come, to offer myself, to do and fulfill your will, because you are my God. Therefore I come to fulfill your will, because so it is written, and prefigured of me in the counsel of the Deity, which is my head, who am the book of the human race according as I am man, in which men may read all things necessary for themselves, and therefore there is no need of the law.
10.8: 10.8 Saying above. As if he said: Not only does this authority note that the old victims did not make perfect, and the victim of Christ alone did; but also the taking away of the Old Testament and the establishment of the New, if the words are diligently noted; because saying above, you would not those, he adds: Then I said. For behold he takes away the first sacrifice and with it the Old Testament, and establishes as stable the new sacrifice and with it the New Testament.
10.10: 10.10 We are sanctified, etc. The purgation of sins being made, we are reconciled to God.
10.11: 10.11 And every, etc. Lest it seem that the blood offered by the high priests once a year profited less and the sacrifices made daily by priests make perfect, he adds this, as if to say: The high priest offering every year does not arrive at consummation, so also every priest always offers, and yet by them is never consummated.
10.12: 10.12 Sits at the right hand. He can well consummate who has so deserved to be exalted.
10.13: 10.13 From henceforth. That is from what remains, namely the glory of the good and the punishment of the wicked. Footstool. Because even if now they resist him, and seem not to be subjected, then to all they will appear subject to him, by whose command they will be under punishments.
10.15: 10.15 And the Holy Ghost also, etc. The Holy Spirit testifies that he has perfected forever the sanctified, and that in the New Testament God will not remember sins. After that. As if to say: After he said what is of no value for our proof, he added other things that confirm both of what we say: namely giving laws, which pertains to consummation; and their sins and iniquities I will remember no more, which pertains to sanctification.
10.16: 10.16 I will write above. He does not say I will write, but I will write above, because those laws are above the strength of men, in the fulfilling of which no one will suffice except by the help of grace. In these words he is said to consummate by virtues, then he adds of sanctification.
10.18: 10.18 Where there is, etc. Not only from this authority can it be seen that Jesus sanctifies and consummates, but that oblation after the time of grace is not to be made for sins, when remission has been made.
10.20: 10.20 Through the veil. Our faith is veiled, because faith has no merit for which human reason supplies experience.
10.22: 10.22 In fullness of faith. Our faith is perfect, since none of these things is now visible, neither priest nor victim. Having our hearts sprinkled. By this it is shown that not faith alone but life with virtue is sought. Washed with water, that is baptism.
10.23: 10.23 For he is faithful. As God is faithful in promises, so he wishes us to be faithful to him in our promises. Let us therefore have faith and confession as far as it is in us.
10.24: 10.24 And let us consider, etc. The perfect by exhorting others, the lesser by imitating the perfect. Hence the Apostle exhorts to what befits faith.
10.25: 10.25 As the manner is. He blames those who cut the unity of charity, as if among others they could not dwell because of their holiness; who rather by their example ought to have consoled them. But comforting. He consoles the laboring who equally persists in the labor, because the relief of labor is the effort, or joint effort, of the fellow-laborer, as happens on a journey.
